solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Makes new recording of Plant’s backing band from Georgia (9)

indicatorNotes.backing: the plant's stands behind the band, supporting it, so it comes second

blocks.note: R.E.M., the rock band from Athens, Georgia
an aster is a plant; ASTER'S = plant's

annotation.surface: Robert Plant re-records with a new backing band from the American South.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Plant' wants to be Robert Plant of Led Zeppelin, which fits the music surface; it is just a flower. Strictly, remastering improves an existing recording rather than making a new one, so the definition is a little loose.
annotation.definitionFit: To remaster is to produce a new master of a recording, a fresh version of the original.

entries.clue: Hairdresser getting educated about American Indian food (5)

indicatorNotes.about: 'about' means surrounding, so RITA is placed around the A

blocks.note: Rita, the hairdresser in the play and film Educating Rita

annotation.surface: A hairdresser goes back to school and learns about Native American cooking.
annotation.walkthrough: 'American Indian' reads as one phrase, but it splits: American is the A and Indian starts the definition. The hairdresser is Rita from Willy Russell's Educating Rita, a hairdresser who takes an Open University course.
annotation.definitionFit: Raita is an Indian side dish of yoghurt with cucumber or other vegetables.

entries.clue: Verbally summoned colonel on board (7)

indicatorNotes.Verbally: spoken rather than written, so a sound-alike

annotation.surface: An officer on a ship is called up by word of mouth.
annotation.walkthrough: 'On board' suggests a ship; the board is the Cluedo game board, where Colonel Mustard is one of the suspects.
annotation.definitionFit: Colonel Mustard is a suspect in the board game Cluedo (Clue in North America).

entries.clue: Baker’s fat and becoming less tall (10)

blocks.note: a baker's fat is the lard or butter rubbed into pastry to make it crumbly
becoming less tall = getting shorter, the present participle of a verb

annotation.surface: A baker is getting plump and shrinking at the same time.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'fat' as an adjective describing the baker; it is a noun, the fat a baker uses. Shortening is that fat, and shortening is also getting shorter.
annotation.definitionFit: Shortening is solid fat such as lard used in baking; shortening also means becoming shorter.

entries.clue: In Essex, trainer bit player (5)

indicatorNotes.In: the answer sits inside the next words

annotation.surface: A racehorse or football trainer in Essex has only a small role.
annotation.walkthrough: Essex is an English county, which makes 'In Essex' look like a place setting rather than an instruction to look inside the words.
annotation.definitionFit: An extra is a performer with a tiny, non-speaking part: a bit player.

entries.clue: Rowdy pals destroyed fencing (9)

indicatorNotes.destroyed: the letters of ROWDY PALS are broken up and rebuilt

annotation.surface: A gang of rowdy friends smashed a garden fence.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fencing' looks like the wooden fence the rowdy pals wrecked; it is the sport.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: fencing is the modern sport built on swordplay, fighting with blades.

entries.clue: Domicile lacking contents and gracious furnishings? (5)

indicatorNotes.lacking contents: the word loses everything inside, keeping its first and last letters

blocks.note: cor! and gracious! are both exclamations of surprise

annotation.surface: An empty home with gracious furnishings sounds like an estate agent's description.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Gracious' reads as an adjective describing furnishings; it is the exclamation, as in 'goodness gracious', which the British COR matches. The question mark flags that furnishings only suggest décor.
annotation.definitionFit: Décor is the furnishing and decoration of a room.

entries.clue: Passes on every second letter from advisers (4)

indicatorNotes.every second letter from: take letters 2, 4, 6 and 8 of the next word

annotation.surface: An instruction to forward every other letter from one's advisers.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Passes on' reads as forwarding the letters; it means dying.
annotation.definitionFit: To pass on is a euphemism for to die, so 'passes on' = dies.

entries.clue: In turmoil, companion starts to avoid obnoxious jerk (7)

indicatorNotes.starts to: take the first letter of each following word

blocks.note: CH = Companion of Honour, a British order
a tic is an involuntary jerk

annotation.surface: A friend in a state of distress tries to steer clear of an unpleasant idiot.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Jerk' looks like an insult for a person; it is a twitch. CH stands for Companion of Honour.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a state of turmoil is one of complete disorder, and a disorderly scene is chaotic.

entries.clue: President massaged lover’s toe (9)

indicatorNotes.massaged: the letters are kneaded into a new shape

annotation.surface: A president gives his lover a foot rub.
annotation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in 'lover's' is ignored, as punctuation always is in cryptic clues.
annotation.definitionFit: Theodore and Franklin D. Roosevelt were both US presidents.

entries.clue: Briefly tense, faced with angry rhinos (2,5)

indicatorNotes.faced with: the rearranged rhinos stand in front of the T
indicatorNotes.angry: the rhinos are stirred up, so their letters move

annotation.surface: A moment of tension when confronted by a crash of furious rhinos.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Tense' reads as nervous; it is the grammatical term, abbreviated T.
annotation.definitionFit: 'In short' and 'briefly' both introduce a summary.

entries.clue: Herb found over in Parsonage Road (7)

indicatorNotes.found: the answer is found within the words that follow
indicatorNotes.over: turned over, so it reads backwards

annotation.surface: A herb has been spotted growing on Parsonage Road.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Over' can look like 'across', but here it tells you to read the hidden letters right to left.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by category: oregano, wild marjoram, is a Mediterranean herb used in cooking.

entries.clue: Daringly unconventional, treated a vagrant with case of dengue (5-5)

indicatorNotes.treated: the letters are processed into a new form
indicatorNotes.case of: only the outside of the word: its first and last letters

blocks.note: DenguE, outer letters, also in the anagram

annotation.surface: A doctor boldly treats a homeless man who has dengue fever.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Treated' and 'case' sit naturally in a medical scene, which hides the fact that one mixes letters and the other takes just the ends of dengue.
annotation.definitionFit: Avant-garde describes art or ideas that are daringly new and experimental.

entries.clue: Filthy place ultimately became eyesore (4)

indicatorNotes.ultimately: at the last, so the final letter

blocks.note: a pigsty, or any filthy place

annotation.surface: A dirty spot eventually turned into an ugly sight.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Eyesore' means an ugly sight in the surface, but is read literally: a sore on the eye.
annotation.definitionFit: A stye is an inflamed swelling on the eyelid, literally a sore on the eye.

entries.clue: Cryptic setter’s beginning to turn in grave (10)

indicatorNotes.beginning to: take the first letter of turn

blocks.note: the setter speaking of himself or herself: my
first letter of Turn, placed inside SERIOUS

annotation.surface: A crossword setter's first clue would make someone turn in their grave.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Turn in grave' reads as the idiom for posthumous disapproval; 'grave' is the adjective. A setter referring to themselves gives ME or MY.
annotation.definitionFit: Cryptic means puzzling or obscure, as does mysterious.

entries.clue: European in exotic land is loaded (5)

indicatorNotes.in: 'in' as a preposition of place puts the European inside the rearranged land
indicatorNotes.exotic: the letters of LAND are made foreign, rearranged

annotation.surface: A European living in a faraway country has become rich.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Loaded' reads as wealthy in the surface; the definition takes its literal sense of carrying a load.
annotation.definitionFit: Laden means loaded, carrying a heavy load.

entries.clue: Left at home with idiot wearing surprised expression and dhoti? (9)

indicatorNotes.wearing: OH has IN and CLOT on it, wrapped inside

blocks.note: oh! as a cry of surprise, going around the next two
clot, British slang for a fool

annotation.surface: Someone left at home with an idiot in a dhoti and a startled look.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Wearing' fits the clothing picture but is the container: the home and the idiot are worn inside the surprised cry. The question mark marks the dhoti as one example of a loincloth.
annotation.definitionFit: A dhoti is the loincloth worn by men in India.

entries.clue: Whine of siren possibly detaining boat, short of time (9)

indicatorNotes.detaining: BELLE holds the boat inside her
indicatorNotes.short of: the boat is missing the T

blocks.note: a siren (seductive woman) might be a belle; 'possibly' flags the example; the boat goes between its two Ls
YACHT minus T (time), placed inside BEL_LE

annotation.surface: The wail of an emergency siren seems to be holding up a boat.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Siren' sounds like an alarm, matching 'whine'; it is a beautiful woman, a belle.
annotation.definitionFit: Informal synonym: to bellyache is to grumble at length, and a whine is exactly that kind of complaint.

entries.clue: Dope and Scotch on top of beer (9)

indicatorNotes.on: in a down clue, BLOCK sits on top of what follows

blocks.note: to scotch a plan is to block it
the head is the foam on top of a beer

annotation.surface: An order at the bar: drugs, a whisky and a beer.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Dope' and 'Scotch' both suggest intoxicants; one means a fool and the other means to thwart. 'Top of beer' is the foam, not the first letter B.
annotation.definitionFit: A dope and a blockhead are both stupid people.

entries.clue: Tesla, perhaps last of many in stock (9)

indicatorNotes.last of: only the final letter of many

blocks.note: Nikola Tesla was an inventor; 'perhaps' marks him as an example

annotation.surface: A car dealer has one of many Tesla cars left in stock.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Tesla' suggests the electric car brand; it is the man it was named after, an inventor.
annotation.definitionFit: Inventory is a stock of goods held by a business.

entries.clue: Invective from learner driver stuck behind six musicians (7)

indicatorNotes.stuck behind: to be stuck behind someone in traffic is to trail them, so the learner comes last

blocks.note: L = learner, from the L-plate on a learner driver's car

annotation.surface: A learner driver stuck in traffic behind a band's van swears at them.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Six musicians' reads as a band of six; the number and the group are separate pieces.
annotation.definitionFit: Vitriol is bitter, abusive speech, the same as invective.

entries.clue: Understood one is bound by discretion (5)

indicatorNotes.is bound by: the I is tied up inside TACT

blocks.note: tact = discretion, going around the I

annotation.surface: Someone understood that they are bound to keep quiet.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Understood' reads as a verb about someone grasping a point; it is the adjective, as in an understood agreement.
annotation.definitionFit: Tacit means understood or implied without being stated.

entries.clue: Who benefits from youngster pinching current Beatle’s wife? (3,4)

indicatorNotes.pinching: CUB grabs the I and holds it inside

blocks.note: a cub is a young animal, or a Cub Scout
I is the symbol for electric current, inside CU_B

annotation.surface: A child steals a Beatle's wife and someone asks who gains.
annotation.walkthrough: Cui bono? is Latin for 'to whose benefit?', a question asked when looking for a motive. I for current comes from physics.
annotation.definitionFit: Cui bono literally means 'for whose good?', asking who benefits.

entries.clue: Animal sanctuary in County Tyrone evacuated (4)

indicatorNotes.evacuated: emptied, leaving only the first and last letters

blocks.note: Co. is the written abbreviation for county, as in Co. Tyrone

annotation.surface: A wildlife refuge in Northern Ireland has been cleared of people.
annotation.walkthrough: County Tyrone is in Northern Ireland and is written Co. Tyrone, so CO comes straight from the name.
annotation.definitionFit: A cote is a shelter for birds or animals, such as a dovecote.

entries.clue: Broadcaster and poet close to having romp (10)

indicatorNotes.close to: the end of the word, its last letter

annotation.surface: A TV presenter and a poet are about to have a fling.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Romp' reads as a sexual encounter in the surface; it means boisterous play. Sky is a British TV company.
annotation.definitionFit: Skylarking is horseplay or boisterous fun, as is a romp.

entries.clue: Gradual decline of northern nomads reported (5)

indicatorNotes.reported: said out loud, so a sound-alike

blocks.note: the Lapps (Sami) are reindeer-herding people of northern Scandinavia

annotation.surface: A news report on the dwindling numbers of Arctic herders.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one phrase about nomads in decline; the break falls after 'decline', with 'of' as the link.
annotation.definitionFit: A lapse is a gradual falling away or decline, as in a lapse into bad habits.

entries.clue: Leaders refused to agree on common land (5)

indicatorNotes.Leaders refused: the first letters are turned away

annotation.surface: Politicians refused to reach agreement over a patch of public land.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Refused to' looks like a single verb phrase; 'Leaders refused' deletes the first letters of the two words after 'to'.
annotation.definitionFit: A village green is common land shared by the community.

entries.clue: Boozer and wife Nora both half-cut (4)

indicatorNotes.both half-cut: each of the two words is cut in half, keeping its first half

annotation.surface: A drunk man and his wife Nora are both tipsy.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Half-cut' is British slang for drunk, which suits the boozer, and here it literally cuts each word in half.
annotation.definitionFit: A wino is a drunkard, especially one who drinks cheap wine.

entries.clue: Our kid intermittently absent following chill in nostril? (7)

indicatorNotes.following: F is the abbreviation for following

blocks.note: f. = following, as in page references

annotation.surface: A child keeps missing school because of a cold in the nose.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Our kid' is northern English for one's younger brother, and reads as a child. 'Following' looks like 'after' but supplies its own F. The question mark marks a nostril as one example of an orifice.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example, flagged by the question mark: a nostril is one of the body's openings, and orifice is the formal word for any such opening.

entries.clue: Mean rugby player with huge energy (7)

blocks.note: a prop is a front-row forward in rugby

annotation.surface: A nasty, huge and energetic rugby forward.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Mean' reads as an adjective (nasty) describing the player; it is the verb, to intend.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the verb sense: 'I mean to go' and 'I propose to go' both state an intention.

entries.clue: Greeting great suffering with love (5)

annotation.surface: Being greeted brings great pain mixed with love.
annotation.walkthrough: Love as O comes from tennis scoring, where love means nil.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: hello is the everyday word said when greeting someone.

entries.clue: Fluff on clothing and carpet (5,4)

indicatorNotes.on: in an across clue, the fluff comes after the clothing

annotation.surface: Lint picked up on your clothes and the rug.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Carpet' looks like the rug gathering fluff; it is the verb, to reprimand, as in 'called on the carpet'.
annotation.definitionFit: To carpet someone is to scold them, which is also to dress them down.
